caveats: MySQL counts errors from when each statement's entry began counting, so old failures stay in its total until the counters are reset or the server restarts.

fix.summary: Another transaction holds the rows it needs for longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout. Find what holds the locks while it waits (Live shows the blocking chain). Keep transactions short. The recent errors and their messages are in performance_schema.

findings.summary: The associated statements used 12.0 s of database time over the 2 minutes since statistics were reset (4%). 12 of its 43 runs since its statistics began 2 minutes ago didn't finish. 12 ended in an error; the recent ones were 1205 lock wait timeout. A run that doesn't finish still costs the time it ran, and the application retries it or shows an error.
findings.title: An update of orders fails 28% of the time (1205 lock wait timeout)
verify: Between two scans, runs that fail or are cancelled should drop to near zero: performance_schema keeps running totals, so compare its failed runs and runs in a scan taken once the change is live and one a day or more later (12 of 43 runs in this scan).

caveats: The statistics don't cover enough time (an hour or more from a known start) to say how many minutes of waiting a day this is, so it isn't raised on its share alone.

fix.summary: Find what holds the locks while it waits (Live shows the blocking chain). Keep the holding transactions short and commit before slow work; make UPDATE and DELETE filter on an index so they lock only the rows they change; touch rows in the same order everywhere.

queries.note: Waited 2 min (nearly all of its time) on locks on shop.orders in the same hours; the holder isn't recorded.

findings.summary: The associated statements used 4 min of database time over the 2 minutes since statistics were reset (80%). Of its 2 min since its statistics began 2 minutes ago, 2 min went to waiting for locks other sessions held. That time belongs to the sessions holding the locks: making this statement faster won't help, shortening the transactions that hold the rows will. MySQL counts row-lock waits in a statement's lock time from 8.0.28; earlier versions count table locks only. An update of orders (query fc709554a9248878) waited on locks on shop.orders on Oct 11, 13:48–14:19 UTC too, 2 min (nearly all of its time): likely the same episode of blocking, behind the same holder or one another.
findings.title: A read from orders spends nearly all its time waiting on locks, 28.8 s per run
verify: Between two scans, its lock time per run should drop: performance_schema keeps running totals, so compare its lock time and runs in a scan taken once the change is live and one a day or more later (2 min over 4 runs in this scan).

caveats: Some high-frequency single-row lookups are legitimate (for example, by primary key on a hot path). Check the calling code before batching.

fix.summary: Reuse a result the application already has, or cache it for as long as it remains valid; access checks must still reflect permission changes. If the caller loops over items, load their rows in one query (WHERE key IN (…) or a join) before the loop; ORMs usually have an eager-loading option for this.

impact.label: 1.1 s of database time over the 2 minutes since statistics were reset (<1%)

findings.summary: 1.1 s of database time over the 2 minutes since statistics were reset (<1%). Its runs are 75% of all statement runs, and each run returns about 1 row. Repeated lookups can be per-request checks or a loop in application code (N+1). Each run is cheap (<1% of database time in all), but each call can add a network round trip.
findings.title: A read from products runs 30K times in 2 minutes, one key at a time
verify: It ran 30K times in 2 minutes. performance_schema keeps running totals, so a later scan's runs, share and averages for this query still hold every run from before the change. Scan when the change ships and again a day or more later, then compare the two in What changed, with Since at the ship time (`culprit changes <connection> --since <ship time>`): there it should run fewer times and take less time in all. A rewritten statement is a new entry with an id of its own, and this one then shows as stopped running.

fix.cost: The limit is per temporary table per connection; size it with your connection count in mind.
fix.sql:
SET PERSIST tmp_table_size = 67108864;
SET PERSIST max_heap_table_size = 67108864;
fix.summary: Check whether an index matching the GROUP BY or ORDER BY reduces temporary-table work (an ORDER BY that differs from the grouping can still need a temporary table and sort), or raise the in-memory limit to 64.0 MB (both variables: with the MEMORY engine the smaller one wins). Set tmp_table_size to 67108864; SET PERSIST keeps it across restarts. Set max_heap_table_size to 67108864; SET PERSIST keeps it across restarts. Global values apply to new connections: reopen the application's existing connections, or have the application set these session variables on them.

findings.summary: The associated statements used 34.5 s of database time over the 2 minutes since statistics were reset (12%). The temporary table behind a GROUP BY, DISTINCT or ORDER BY in this statement outgrows the in-memory limit (1.0 MB, the smaller of tmp_table_size and max_heap_table_size, where these tables use the MEMORY engine; the TempTable engine stops at tmp_table_size and temptable_max_ram instead) and moves to disk, which is many times slower: 20 on-disk tables in 20 runs.
findings.title: A read from orders builds an on-disk temporary table about once per run
verify: Once the application's connections use the new limits, its on-disk temporary tables should stop growing while its runs go on: performance_schema keeps running totals, so compare its on-disk temporary tables and runs in a scan taken once the change is live and one a day or more later (20 in 20 runs in this scan).

caveats: Counters accumulate since statistics were last reset; one nightly report can make up much of them.

fix.cost: shop.orders had no writes in what its counters cover, which may be short: performance_schema's counters start over when they are reset, and a weekly job may not have run since; each write it gets will also update any index you add.
fix.summary: Explain the statements listed with this finding to check their access paths. To measure each filter, capture an actual plan with representative values in a controlled environment: this runs the statement. Compare rows kept with rows read. If a filter keeps at most 10% of the rows read, consider an index on the columns it searches by; if it keeps more, read fewer rows or columns instead. Small lookup tables are fine to scan.

findings.summary: The associated statements used 4.3 s of database time over the 2 minutes since statistics were reset (1%). shop.orders has 499K rows, and queries have read all of it 81 times since the server started or its performance_schema counters were last reset: 40.5M rows read without an index. 1 of the captured statements reads it in full (its plan scans it); explain it to check the access path, then measure rows kept in representative runs. A read from orders (query 04cd7be9c366fadc) reads it in full too, on purpose: it has no WHERE clause, so no index on a filter changes that.
findings.title: orders is read in full 81 times since the server started or its performance_schema counters were last reset (40.5M rows)
verify: After adding an index for a selective filter, the full reads of orders should grow far slower. Compare how much its scan counters grow between a scan taken once the change is live and one a day or more later (81 full reads in this scan).

Whether the fix adds an index or reads fewer rows or columns: performance_schema keeps running totals, so a later scan's runs, share and averages for the query still hold every run from before the change. Scan when the change ships and again a day or more later, then compare the two in What changed, with Since at the ship time (`culprit changes <connection> --since <ship time>`): there its time per run should drop.

caveats: ix_orders_status is narrower, so scans of it read fewer pages. Keep it if a hot query scans it rather than seeking.

fix.sql: ALTER TABLE `shop`.`orders` DROP INDEX `ix_orders_status`, ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE;

findings.summary: ix_orders_status has keys (status) and ix_orders_status_created has keys (status, created_at). Any query that can seek on ix_orders_status can seek on ix_orders_status_created instead. Every write to shop.orders maintains both.
findings.title: ix_orders_status is covered by the wider ix_orders_status_created on orders
verify: Re-scan after removing ix_orders_status: this finding should be gone, and ix_orders_status_created should still exist.

Compare queries on shop.orders over comparable periods before and after the change, under a similar workload: their time per run should stay the same or drop. If a query gets slower, check its plan before keeping the index removed.

fix.sql: ALTER TABLE `shop`.`products` DROP INDEX `ix_products_sku`, ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE;

findings.summary: ix_products_sku has keys (sku) and uq_products_sku has keys (sku). They are the same index twice. Every write to shop.products maintains both.
findings.title: ix_products_sku duplicates uq_products_sku on products
verify: Re-scan after removing ix_products_sku: this finding should be gone, and uq_products_sku should still exist.

Compare queries on shop.products over comparable periods before and after the change, under a similar workload: their time per run should stay the same or drop. If a query gets slower, check its plan before keeping the index removed.

caveats: MySQL counts row-lock waits for the whole server, so other databases' waits are in these numbers.

fix.summary: Keep transactions short (no user input or slow calls inside them), make UPDATE and DELETE filter on indexed columns, and touch tables in the same order everywhere. Live shows who blocks whom right now.

findings.summary: Since MySQL started 80 minutes ago, InnoDB made transactions across the whole server (it counts every database together) wait for row locks 6 times, 1 min 27 s in all and about 14.5 s each: about 1 min an hour on average; the counters don't say when. In this database, a read from orders waited longest on locks (2 min in total). Lock waits grow with long transactions, and with UPDATE or DELETE statements whose filter isn't indexed: they lock every row they scan.
findings.title: Transactions on this server waited 1 min 27 s for row locks since MySQL started 80 minutes ago, 14.5 s each on average
verify: Sample Waits → Right now during normal load: it counts row-lock waits over the sample, which should be rare and short.

fix.summary: Return only what's used: page the results (keyset pagination, or LIMIT / OFFSET … FETCH), filter in SQL rather than in the application, select only the columns you need, and aggregate in the database.

findings.summary: The associated statements used 82 ms of database time over the 2 minutes since statistics were reset (<1%). Each run sends 20K rows to the application; its 25 runs since its statistics began 2 minutes ago moved 500K rows. Few screens or jobs need that many at once: the database reads them, the network carries them and the application holds them in memory.
findings.title: A read from order_items returns 20K rows per run
verify: Between two scans, the rows it returns per run should drop to what a page or a job actually uses: performance_schema keeps running totals, so compare its rows and runs in a scan taken once the change is live and one a day or more later (500K rows in 25 runs in this scan).

fix.summary: Turn it on with a threshold that matches your latency budget. Set slow_query_log to ON, long_query_time to 1 and log_output to FILE,TABLE; SET PERSIST keeps it across restarts. The new long_query_time applies to new connections: reopen the application's existing connections, or have the application set the session variable on them.

findings.summary: Without it there is no record of individual slow statements with their real parameter values, only the aggregated digests. Logged to the mysql.slow_log table, Culprit also uses those statements to plan digests that have no sample text.
findings.title: The slow query log is off
verify: Re-scan once the change has taken effect: this finding is gone.

check.description: Repeated SQL shapes correlated by explicit request_id in structured logs. Repetition identifies a caller to inspect; it does not prove an N+1 bug or removable work.
check.title: Repeated statements within logged requests

deadlocks.note: InnoDB keeps only its most recent deadlock. Turn on innodb_print_all_deadlocks to write every one to the error log.

signals.healthy: An average across the whole server's recorded row-lock waits, not a current wait. The lock findings use the amount of waiting too.

items.detail: The rows don't arrive in the order the GROUP BY / DISTINCT needs, so MySQL builds a temporary table (on disk once it outgrows tmp_table_size) and sorts the result.
items.fix: An index whose leading columns match the GROUP BY may let MySQL group in index order and reduce grouping work. An ORDER BY that differs from the grouping, especially an aggregate such as COUNT(*) DESC, can still need a temporary table and sort. Filter rows before grouping, or keep a pre-aggregated result, to reduce that work.
items.title: Groups 499K rows in an internal temporary table, then sorts them (filesort)
items.verify: Explain again: look for grouping in index order or fewer rows entering the temporary table. A temporary table and sort for a different ORDER BY can remain; compare on-disk temporary tables on new runs to check the spill itself.
